title: Surface Integral
body:
Integrating over a two-dimensional surface sitting in three-dimensional space. Exactly the
[[Line Integral]] story one dimension up: two kinds, scalar and vector, and both are evaluated by
[[Parameterization|parameterising]] and reducing to a [[Double Integral]] over the parameter
domain.

## Scalar: $\iint_S f\,dS$

$$
\iint_S f\,dS = \iint_D f(\mathbf{r}(u,v))\,\|\mathbf{r}_u \times \mathbf{r}_v\|\,du\,dv
$$

Take $f = 1$ and you get the **area** of the surface, the way $\int_C ds$ gives the length of a
curve. Use it for the mass of a thin shell of variable density.

## Vector: $\iint_S \mathbf{F}\cdot d\mathbf{S}$

$$
\iint_S \mathbf{F}\cdot d\mathbf{S} = \iint_D \mathbf{F}\cdot(\mathbf{r}_u \times \mathbf{r}_v)\,du\,dv
$$

This is the [[Flux]] of $\mathbf{F}$ through $S$: how much of the field passes **through** the
surface rather than sliding along it. The [[Dot Product]] with the normal is what discards the
tangential part.

| | Line integral | Surface integral |
|---|---|---|
| Domain | curve, one parameter | surface, two parameters |
| Scalar element | $ds = \lVert\mathbf{r}'\rVert\,dt$ | $dS = \lVert\mathbf{r}_u \times \mathbf{r}_v\rVert\,du\,dv$ |
| Vector element | $d\mathbf{r} = \mathbf{r}'dt$ | $d\mathbf{S} = (\mathbf{r}_u \times \mathbf{r}_v)\,du\,dv$ |
| Vector version measures | work, circulation **along** | flux **through** |
| Orientation | direction of travel | which side is "out" |

## Orientation

A surface has two sides and you have to commit to one. The cross product
$\mathbf{r}_u \times \mathbf{r}_v$ picks a normal, and swapping $u$ and $v$ reverses it, so the
sign of a flux integral is a choice you make and then have to keep. Convention for a **closed**
surface: the normal points **outward**, which is what [[Divergence Theorem|the divergence theorem]]
assumes.

Not every surface can be oriented. A Möbius band has one side, so "flux through it" is not a
well-formed question, which is the reason orientability appears in the hypotheses of
[[Stokes' Theorem]] rather than being assumed silently.
